extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers (contemporary 1945 audience); readers of wartime/military news
extracted.subtask_description: A newspaper obituary/feature chronicling the death, career, personality, controversies, and public reactions to a senior military figure (here, Gen. George S. Patton, Jr.). Often combines death notice, biographical summary, battlefield accomplishments, anecdotes, and official/public statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report precise circumstances and timing of death
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish the official announcement with precise time/place and immediate medical bulletins (example verbatim: “General Patton died at 5.50 P.M. today… The General died peacefully.”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include hospital bulletins, chronology of deterioration, specific medical complications (e.g., pulmonary congestion, spinal-cord injury, paralysis, weakened heart), and short timeline from accident to death so readers understand cause and proximate events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide authoritative medical/condition updates
rubrics_metrics.description: Include intermediate bulletins on condition (e.g., “General Patton’s condition is considered serious… pulmonary complication … accumulation of secretions in the lungs … paralysis of one side of the diaphragm…”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote medical bulletins or statements from attending surgeons/medical consultants and show progression (serious → grave → death), giving clinical detail sufficient to explain how death occurred without excessive technicality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summarize major military career and achievements
rubrics_metrics.description: Chronicle service and campaigns (Africa, Sicily, Normandy, the Saar, Seine, Loire, Moselle, Saar, Rhine, Danube, Siegfried Line, capture of Metz; 3d Army’s movements and accomplishments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List theaters, notable campaigns and battles, awards and recognitions, and quantifiable impacts (territory liberated, prisoners captured, casualties inflicted) to establish the subject’s significance in military history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include reactions and statements from leaders and contemporaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish statements from heads of state and senior military/political leaders (example: President Truman’s message: “MrsTruman and I extend our deepest sympathy to you…”; Eisenhower’s statement praising his leadership).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present a range of official condolences and assessments (president, chiefs of staff, senators, congressional leaders) to convey national significance and tone; attribute all quotes clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record eyewitness/colleague testimonies and anecdotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate remarks and recollections from officers and those who served with him (e.g., Maj. Gen. John W. O’Daniel, Brig. Gen. Ogden J. Ross) and vivid campaign scenes (e.g., Patton’s jeep with air-horn, leading from the front).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use short, attributed anecdotes and color detail to humanize the subject and illustrate leadership style; these should support the biographical narrative without replacing factual chronology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present family and personal biographical details
rubrics_metrics.description: Give age, birthplace, schooling, survivors (wife, son Lt. George S. Patton, 3rd, two daughters), funeral arrangements and where family will be taken (e.g., Heidelberg for funeral).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include personal background (birth date/place, education, interests), immediate family names and locations, and practical funeral/visitation information that readers expect in an obituary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge controversies and corrective actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Document criticisms and public controversies (soldier-slapping incident, denazification program criticism, relieved commands) and institutional responses (public apology, corrective actions, relief from command).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide balanced coverage: state the incident, contemporary reactions (Congress, Army), any apologies or official findings, and later context showing rehabilitation or continuing controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vivid narrative lead and scene-setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Open with descriptive scenes or a strong narrative hook (examples: descriptions of the Sicilian campaign, Patton’s statement “Gentlemen, I have asked you to do the difficult before. This time I'm asking the impossible.”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ evocative language and direct quotes to draw readers in while ensuring factual accuracy; combine scene-setting with immediate facts about the death to satisfy both interest and information needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide context via quantifiable operational specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: Include operational statistics and outcomes to show impact (e.g., Third Army claimed a large number of the 60,000 German casualties; captured more than 750,000 Nazi soldiers; liberated 80,000 square miles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use verified figures and concrete metrics where available to quantify the subject’s military significance; attribute or qualify numbers if estimates or claims are reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute reporting and note correspondent perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify news organization and reporters’ roles (e.g., “Editor’s Note: Ball, Associated Press correspondent, covered Gen. George S. Patton…”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly attribute pieces, note when material includes a correspondent’s firsthand coverage or an editor’s compilation, and separate reported facts from anecdotal or subjective characterizations.
